title: Aquaculture-derived carbon and nitrogen fuel N<sub>2</sub>O emissions and undermine mangrove climate benefits.
abstract: This study revealed the effects of aquaculture activities on sediment N<sub>2</sub>O emissions in Zhangjiang Estuary mangrove, southeastern China: (1) the annual average emission rate of N<sub>2</sub>O was 0.073 t ha<sup>-1</sup> yr<sup>-1</sup> (19.82 t CO<sub>2</sub> eq ha<sup>-1</sup> yr<sup>-1</sup>), offsetting about 43.08% of the climate benefits produced by the carbon sequestration here; (2) Aquaculture-derived NO<sub>3</sub> <sup>-</sup> directly provided substrate for sediment denitrification. Nitrogen inputs with high NH<sub>4</sub> <sup>+</sup>: NO<sub>3</sub> <sup>-</sup> ratios also led to the NO<sub>2</sub> <sup>-</sup> accumulation in the overlying water and sediment pore water, further promoting denitrification. In addition, the input of highly reactive organic matter from aquaculture could directly stimulate denitrification, or indirectly promote it by supporting CH<sub>4</sub> oxidation; (3) Although denitrification was accelerated by aquaculture activities, the reduction of N<sub>2</sub>O was likely inhibited by the acidic conditions of the study area, thus increasing N<sub>2</sub>O emissions. This study highlights the need to incorporate sustainable aquaculture management into mangrove conservation frameworks.
